## Does anything actually treat infant colic?

**TL;DR** — Colic is common, has no established cause, and resolves on its own by month three to four. One probiotic strain buys breastfed babies about 25 minutes less crying a day; the largest trial found no benefit at all, and every other common remedy fails its tests. The strongest intervention is supporting the parents until it passes.

### Colic is common, defined by a stopwatch, and ends on its own

- The classic definition is the "rule of threes": crying or fussing ≥3 hours a day, ≥3 days a week, for ≥3 weeks in a healthy, thriving infant [@GutirrezCastrelln2017efficacy].
- The Rome IV criteria drop the stopwatch: prolonged, unexplained crying in a thriving infant [@Benninga2016childhood].
- The two most rigorous community surveys put cumulative incidence at 5–19%, with no link to sex, social class, or feeding type [@Lucassen2001systematic].
- Crying peaks around week six and fades by month three to four in virtually all infants, treated or not [@GutirrezCastrelln2017efficacy; @Hjern2020systematic].

### The cause is unknown; the gut is the prime suspect

- No mechanism is established; gas, temperament, and parenting were never convicted [@Zeevenhooven2018infant].
- Colicky infants show raised faecal calprotectin and fewer *Bifidobacterium* whatever their feeding mode [@Rhoads2018infant].
- Baseline gut-bacteria composition partly predicts which infants will still be crying a month later [@Loughman2021infant].
- Children who were colicky babies have five- to six-fold higher odds of later migraine — some colic may be an early pain syndrome [@Gelfand2015relationship].

### One probiotic strain helps — but only breastfed babies

- Pooled individual data from four double-blind trials: −25.4 min/day crying at day 21, number needed to treat 2.6 in breastfed infants [@Sung2018lactobacillus].
- The largest, strictest trial (167 infants, first to include formula-fed): no benefit, and 49 min/day *more* fussing [@Sung2014treating].
- European guidance now recommends the strain for breastfed colicky infants only, and nothing for formula-fed ones [@Szajewska2023probiotics].
- {{figure:colic-treatments}} plots the three verdicts side by side.

![Three dot-and-whisker rows on one minutes-per-day axis: pooled L. reuteri left of zero, the largest trial right of zero, lactase straddling it.](colic-treatments.png)

**Figure {#colic-treatments}. The best treatment helps some babies — and failed its biggest test.**
- **Shows:** Reported change in daily crying/fussing versus placebo for the pooled probiotic trials, the largest single trial, and pooled lactase trials.
- **Evidence boundary:** Different populations and feeding modes — three separate verdicts, not one pooled effect.
- **Sources:** [@Sung2018lactobacillus; @Sung2014treating; @KozowskaJalowska2024effect]

### Everything else fails its tests

- Simethicone (gas drops): no benefit over placebo; proton pump inhibitors: not supported [@Ellwood2020comparison].
- Dietary changes (hydrolysed formula, low-allergen maternal diet): low-quality evidence only [@Gordon2018dietary].
- Lactase drops: no significant effect in pooled trials [@KozowskaJalowska2024effect].
- Chiropractic and osteopathic manipulation: the effect disappears in parent-blinded trials [@Dobson2012manipulative].

### The real burden lands on parents — and it ends

- Inconsolable crying quadruples the odds of maternal depressive symptoms at two months [@Radesky2013inconsolable].
- In a survey of 3,259 families, 5.6% of parents admitted smothering, slapping, or shaking their baby because of crying [@Reijneveld2004infant].
- Long-term outcomes show associations only — more adolescent indigestion-type complaints, no proven lasting harm [@Zeevenhooven2024functional; @Indrio2023infantile].
- Every guideline starts with parental reassurance, not a prescription [@Ellwood2020comparison].
